cases.title: Disability Intergroup Reviews Key Disability Rights Priorities

article_facts.main_actor: Members of the European Parliament Disability Intergroup and the European Disability Forum
article_facts.principal_development: The Intergroup reviewed disability-rights implementation priorities and areas for joint advocacy.
article_facts.disabled_community: Disabled people represented by the European disability movement
article_facts.specific_concern: Implementation of disability rights in housing, artificial intelligence, digital networks and the next EU budget
article_facts.event_status: Completed meeting; future advocacy priorities identified
article_facts.geographic_scope: European Union and the wider European disability movement
article_facts.qualifications: The evidence records priorities and calls for action; it does not establish that the proposed policy changes have been adopted.

verified_facts.fact: Intergroup members called for stronger implementation of disability rights and discussed the Enhanced Disability Rights Strategy.
The meeting considered housing, artificial intelligence and the EU simplification agenda as issues affecting disabled people.
The update identified the next EU budget and Digital Networks Act as priorities for joint work with the disability movement.

eligibility.category_evidence: Collective disability-rights advocacy and policy demands define the article.
eligibility.geography_evidence: The article concerns EU institutions and the European disability movement; Global is retained as non-geographic scope in the benchmark contract.

cases.title: Will the House of Lords improve accessibility in the Railways Bill?

article_facts.main_actor: Transport for All and members of the House of Lords
article_facts.principal_development: The Railways Bill reached the House of Lords, where amendments could strengthen accessibility duties and disabled passengers' rights.
article_facts.specific_concern: Legal rights, accessibility duties and the future operation of the rail network
article_facts.qualifications: Potential amendments and duties were under consideration; stronger legal rights had not been enacted.

verified_facts.fact: The Railways Bill was before the House of Lords, where amendments could improve how railways operate for disabled passengers.
The Bill creates Great British Railways and other public bodies responsible for shaping the future rail network.
House of Commons proposals for stronger legal rights were not adopted; a government factsheet instead described an accessibility duty and consideration of disabled passengers' needs.

eligibility.category_evidence: The central issue is disabled passengers' access and legal rights in transport.
eligibility.geography_evidence: The legislation and rail system are UK-wide; United Kingdom maps to Northern Europe.

cases.title: BCA calls for calm in smart glasses ban debate

article_facts.principal_development: The organisation responded to calls for smart-glasses bans and warned that hostile debate was making blind and partially sighted users feel unsafe.
article_facts.specific_concern: Smart glasses used as assistive technology and proposed public-facility bans
article_facts.event_status: Public debate and local ad hoc bans underway
article_facts.qualifications: The article reports safety concerns and assistive uses; it does not establish that all smart glasses are assistive or that a nationwide ban exists.

verified_facts.fact: Blind Citizens Australia warned that calls to ban smart glasses were putting blind and partially sighted people in danger.
The organisation described smart glasses as assistive technology that can combine several platforms in one wearable device.
Members and other users reported feeling unsafe using the devices in public, while some councils had introduced ad hoc bans at facilities.

eligibility.category_evidence: Assistive smart-glasses technology and its use by blind people define the article.
eligibility.geography_evidence: Blind Citizens Australia and Australian council actions support Australia, which maps to Oceania.

cases.title: Time to grow: exploring disability justice and climate justice through The Secret Gardens

article_facts.main_actor: Creative Access Dramaturg Kate Lovell, writer Tom Wentworth and The Egg theatre
article_facts.principal_development: A disabled-led adaptation and long-term producing process reworked The Secret Garden through disability justice and climate justice.
article_facts.disabled_community: Disabled artists and audiences, including a wheelchair-using character and a neurodivergent interpretation of Mary
article_facts.specific_concern: Reclaiming a cure narrative, embedding the social model of disability and developing access through slow producing
article_facts.event_status: Stage run completed; wider engagement and a filmed production continued
article_facts.qualifications: The article reflects the author's work on the project; it presents an artistic and producing approach rather than a measured general outcome.

verified_facts.fact: Tom Wentworth's adaptation at The Egg reimagined The Secret Garden through a disabled perspective with a disabled team, presented Mary as neurodivergent and rejected the original cure ending for wheelchair-using Colin.
Kate Lovell worked as Creative Access Dramaturg from 2022, beginning with disability-equality training and continuing through script development, research and access consultation.
The longer project connected disability justice with climate justice and extended into work with schools, children in hospital and a filmed production.

eligibility.category_evidence: A disabled-led theatre adaptation and its creative process are the central subject.
eligibility.geography_evidence: The production was based at The Egg in Bath, United Kingdom; United Kingdom maps to Northern Europe.

article_facts.main_actor: Artists in the Poole-based 15 Days In Clay project
article_facts.principal_development: The project presented Edible Conversation, a ceramics exhibition shaped by learning-disabled artists' work and experiences.
article_facts.disabled_community: Adults with learning disabilities and additional needs who participate as ceramic artists
article_facts.specific_concern: An exhibition using animal totems, clay food and worry monsters to express affirmation, belonging and harmful experiences
article_facts.event_status: Exhibition underway when the article was published
article_facts.geographic_scope: Poole and Swanage, Dorset, United Kingdom
article_facts.qualifications: The article describes the project and artists' work; broad claims about impact should be attributed or expressed with restraint.

verified_facts.fact: 15 Days In Clay has supported adults with learning disabilities and additional needs to develop as ceramic artists since 2003 and had grown to four days a week with more than 40 participants.
Edible Conversation featured five-foot animal totems, a clay banquet carrying positive words and contrasting worry monsters based on artists' lived experiences.
A four-foot revolving ceramic cake traced the project's previous group shows, while the exhibition included work by up to 40 artists.

eligibility.category_evidence: The work, exhibition and development of learning-disabled ceramic artists define the article.
eligibility.geography_evidence: The project is based in Poole and the exhibition was in Swanage, United Kingdom; United Kingdom maps to Northern Europe.

cases.title: Paid Commission for DPOs | Contribute to sector-changing research on DPO Funding

article_facts.main_actor: Trust for London, Disability Rights UK and Braw Data
article_facts.principal_development: The partners invited Disabled People's Organisations to verify their classification and funding information for a UK-wide funding map.
article_facts.disabled_community: Disabled People's Organisations and led-by-and-for organisations
article_facts.specific_concern: Evidence for funding justice, sector connection and campaigning by Disabled People's Organisations
article_facts.event_status: Research and paid participation opportunity underway
article_facts.qualifications: The project was collecting verification data; the map and research findings were not yet complete.

verified_facts.fact: Trust for London, Disability Rights UK and Braw Data were collaborating on UK-wide research mapping funding to the disability sector and a larger map of Disabled People's Organisations.
The project was intended to support campaigners promoting funding justice for Disabled People's Organisations and led-by-and-for organisations.
Disabled People's Organisations were offered £50 to complete a 30-minute form confirming their classification and funding sources.

eligibility.category_evidence: Disabled-led sector research and its intended use in campaigning for funding justice make Activism the strongest category.
eligibility.geography_evidence: The project is explicitly UK-wide; United Kingdom maps to Northern Europe.
